{"id": "16:36/q16", "question": "Why is the verb feminine in haqqat, unlike comparable wording elsewhere?", "turns_on": "Whether agreement is explained by grammatical distance and the feminine antecedent, or by a contrast between worldly deviation and afterlife punishment.", "positions": [{"id": "16:36/q16/p1", "position": "Feminine agreement fits the feminine subject and the feminine community implied by minhum; the comparison has more separation and a masculine equivalent.", "reasons": "Burhan compares 7:30, saying min refers to umma and greater verb-subject separation there better licenses omission. Itqan states the general rule for a truly feminine subject, adds that more intervening words favor omission, and contrasts feminine umma with masculine fariq, citing 3:113. Samarrai notes that masculine agreement can follow a masculine intended sense."}, {"id": "16:36/q16/p2", "position": "Feminine agreement signals worldly misguidance itself; masculine agreement elsewhere signals afterlife punishment.", "reasons": "Samarrai distinguishes worldly contexts, where misguidance remains real, from the afterlife, where realities become clear and the intended masculine sense is punishment; he cites 7:29. The two Lamasat passages repeat the semantic-agreement argument."}]}
{"id": "16:36/q17", "question": "How is the nūn vowel in an iʿbudu read and explained?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "16:36/q17/p1", "position": "A kasra breaks the meeting of two consonants at rest; a damma may follow the preceding vowel or the vowel in ʿibāda.", "reasons": "The qiraat note gives both phonological explanations, without naming a reader in the supplied text."}]}
{"id": "16:36/q18", "question": "Who is addressed by the command to travel?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "16:36/q18/p1", "position": "The present polytheist deniers, especially Quraysh or Mecca's unbelievers; the warning also applies more widely.", "reasons": "Muqatil names Mecca's disbelievers; Baydawi, Bursevi and Alusi name Quraysh or the polytheists. Study Quran particularly identifies Arabs who reportedly passed ruined sites in travel, while extending the command more broadly. Biqai addresses doubters of the messengers."}]}
{"id": "16:36/q19", "question": "What should travel and looking at the deniers' fate teach?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "16:36/q19/p1", "position": "Inspect the ruins of earlier deniers, reflect, and take warning that the same punishment may overtake present deniers.", "reasons": "Tabari, Thalabi, Baghawi, Qurṭubi and Nasafi describe ruined homes and divine destruction; Wahidi, Ibn al-Jawzi, Razi, Tabrisi and Biqai emphasize reflection, proof and warning. Ibn Kathir says the earlier disobedient were punished after warning and cites 47:10 and 67:18. Baydawi, Bursevi and Alusi name Ad and Thamud; Biqai adds later peoples and their dwellings, plus inherited stories from disbelieving ancestors. Study Quran cites travel parallels 3:137, 6:11, 27:69, 30:42 and the general value of journeying at 30:9. Ibn Atiyya urges investigation; Abu Hayyan says inspection confirms rejection's outcome."}]}
{"id": "16:36/q20", "question": "What fate did the deniers meet?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "16:36/q20/p1", "position": "Worldly ruin and destruction through punishment, with the Fire following for the deniers.", "reasons": "Yahya reports Qatada's sequence of destruction then Fire; Muqatil points to visible remains of this-world punishment; Thalabi, Baghawi, Qurṭubi, Nasafi, and others describe devastated lands or homes. Ibn Atiyya allows worldly punishment or Hell as the decisive end; Razi reports al-Jubbai using the destroyed nations to explain misguidance as punishment."}]}
{"id": "16:36/q21", "question": "What rhetorical force do the order, fa, and question about the fate carry?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "16:36/q21/p1", "position": "The sequence turns the division into an urgent, visible proof: guided people are mentioned first, then the audience is directed at once to ask about and inspect deniers' end.", "reasons": "Biqai says mentioning the guided first supports the following claim about those fixed in error, and that direct address follows a proof accessible to insight because sensory evidence remains; he says the fa indicates immediate action unlike slower thumma in 6:11, and kayfa prompts inquiry. Bursevi also takes fa as urging prompt reflection; Alusi says the travel command follows misguidance without spelling out punishment because the result is obvious, and its second fa urges saving reflection. Alusi also analyzes the fa of fa-minhum as explanatory or resumptive after an omitted consequence."}]}
{"id": "16:36/q22", "question": "How does the verse connect to 16:35 and the surrounding passage?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "16:36/q22/p1", "position": "It explains that messengers clearly deliver God's universal command, rebuts the polytheists' excuse, and sets past guided and ruined peoples before the present audience.", "reasons": "Ibn Atiyya and Abu Hayyan connect it to 16:35's limit on messengers' duty; Ibn Ashur says it develops that rebuttal and the earlier example of predecessors. Biqai says an earlier plural for messengers implies distribution, made explicit here; it answers the expected question, rebuts objections, consoles the Prophet, and urges reflection. Tabatabai ties the universal practice to the preceding verse. Alusi questions two proposed interpretive hints and whether a division must be exclusive, especially if the following clause answers part of the first objection. Samarrai says the universal call to worship fits al-Nahl's worship context. Abu Hayyan reports an alternative connection in which li-yubayyina refers to sending a messenger to every nation to expose disagreement and former error."}]}
{"id": "16:36/q23", "question": "What ancillary lexical and report material appears in the supplied notes?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "16:36/q23/p1", "position": "Ibn al-Jawzi's adjoining lexical notes treat food and prompting, and report the Prophet's description of Zamzam and a recitation-prompting instruction.", "reasons": "Ibn al-Jawzi says ta'am means food, ta'imtu 'I tasted,' istaṭʿama al-hadith asks for narration, ta'im can describe someone well fed, mit'am a frequent host or heavy eater, muṭ'am one provided for, and tu'ma food or livelihood. A bow is muṭ'ima because it brings game, illustrated by Dhu al-Rumma's verse. He reports the Prophet calling Zamzam satisfying food and a cure, and a report telling congregants to prompt an imam who requests it. These notes do not explain a word of 16:36."}]}
{"id": "16:36/q24", "question": "Why are deniers accountable although their acts occur within God's will?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "16:36/q24/p1", "position": "Their chosen disobedience of the messengers violates God's command and establishes the proof against them by ordinary human standards.", "reasons": "Biqai distinguishes the occurrence of their choice within God's will from their own choice to disobey, for which they are answerable."}]}
{"id": "16:78/q01", "question": "How does this verse connect to its surrounding passage?", "turns_on": "Whether the connection is made through earlier gifts, the Hour, or what follows.", "positions": [{"id": "16:78/q01/p1", "position": "It continues the proofs of God's oneness through His gifts and power.", "reasons": "Al-Ālūsī prefers coordination with the making of spouses in 16:72; al-Ṭībī instead connects it to God's unlimited power in 16:77. Ṭabāṭabāʾī sees the sequence of favors as proofs of lordship, resurrection, prophecy, and legislation. Study Quran compares the bringing forth of milk (16:66), honey (16:69), and the Hour (16:77)."}, {"id": "16:78/q01/p2", "position": "First creation from the womb proves the possibility of the Hour and resurrection.", "reasons": "Abū Ḥayyān says the Hour and human ignorance have just been mentioned. Biqāʿī says the Creator who formed people in the inaccessible womb can bring them from earth still more readily. Bayḍāwī points from gradual creation to God's power even to raise creatures all at once."}, {"id": "16:78/q01/p3", "position": "The next bird verse follows by inference from this act of bringing forth.", "reasons": "Al-Burhān explains why 16:79 begins without a conjunction; Abū Ḥayyān says the bird passage selects sight as an especially striking means of perceiving creation."}, {"id": "16:78/q01/p4", "position": "The faculties prepare readers to reflect on the subjects in the following verses.", "reasons": "Kur'an Yolu says reflection draws lessons toward good; al-Nasafī calls the next verse another proof of God's power."}]}
{"id": "16:78/q02", "question": "What does God's bringing people from their mothers' wombs show?", "turns_on": "Which divine attribute or consequence the act is taken to demonstrate.", "positions": [{"id": "16:78/q02/p1", "position": "It displays divine power to create and resurrect.", "reasons": "Bayḍāwī reasons from gradual creation to God's power to raise all at once; Biqāʿī compares bringing people from the earth with bringing them from wombs, and stresses the inaccessible place where faculties were formed."}, {"id": "16:78/q02/p2", "position": "It reveals the one knowing, powerful, freely acting benefactor.", "reasons": "Biqāʿī argues natural forces are themselves created and act only as God directs; the signs invite acknowledgment of the messengers' teaching."}]}
{"id": "16:78/q03", "question": "What does أُمَّهَٰت mean, and how is its form explained?", "turns_on": "Whether the discussion concerns the added letter alone or a usage distinction between human and animal mothers.", "positions": [{"id": "16:78/q03/p1", "position": "It is the plural of mother, with an added hāʾ or tāʾ; أمات is the shorter form.", "reasons": "Al-Zajjāj, Thaʿlabī, Jishumī, Abū Isḥāq via Ibn ʿAṭiyya, Ṭabrisī, Rāzī, Qurṭubī, Nasafī, Bursevī, and Ṭabāṭabāʾī compare أهرقت/إه

راق with أرقت/أراق. Al-Ālūsī cites الأمومة and Qusayy ibn Kilāb's أمهتي; he calls singular addition rare and verbal addition rarer. Samīn refers readers to his earlier discussion in al-Nisāʾ."}, {"id": "16:78/q03/p2", "position": "The longer form is used of human mothers, the shorter of animal mothers.", "reasons": "Al-Ālūsī reports this marked versus unmarked usage; Ṭabāṭabāʾī reports the same distinction as a saying."}]}
{"id": "16:78/q04", "question": "How is أُمَّهَٰتِكُمْ read?", "turns_on": "Which vowels or omitted hamza a reader transmits; some sources differ in assigning the variants.", "positions": [{"id": "16:78/q04/p1", "position": "The initial hamza and mīm both take kasra.", "reasons": "Ḥamza is assigned this reading by Thaʿlabī, Baghawī, Ibn al-Jawzī, Qurṭubī, Abū Ḥayyān, al-Nashr, and al-Ālūsī; Thaʿlabī and Qurṭubī also name al-Aʿmash, and Qurṭubī names Ibn Waththāb. The Kisaʾī/Hamza summaries in Jishumī, Rāzī, Ibn ʿAṭiyya, and Qirāʾāt-ER vary in detail. Al-Nashr says this applies in connected reading across four occurrences; Ibn al-Jawzī names 24:61, 39:6, 53:32."}, {"id": "16:78/q04/p2", "position": "The initial hamza takes kasra and the mīm fatḥa.", "reasons": "Al-Kisāʾī is named by Thaʿlabī, Ibn al-Jawzī, Qurṭubī, Abū Ḥayyān, and al-Nashr; explanations include dialect or vowel assimilation. Baghawī, Ibn ʿAṭiyya, Jishumī, Rāzī, Bayḍāwī, and Nasafī report the hamza's kasra less precisely; al-Ālūsī's summary instead assigns kasra to al-Kisāʾī's mīm. Qirāʾāt-ER gives the intermediate vowel form."}, {"id": "16:78/q04/p3", "position": "The initial hamza takes ḍamma and the mīm fatḥa.", "reasons": "Thaʿlabī, Baghawī, Ibn al-Jawzī, and Qurṭubī assign it to the remaining readers; Qurṭubī calls the hamza's ḍamma original. Ibn al-Jawzī says the readings recur at 24:61, 39:6, and 53:32, with no disagreement when beginning recitation."}, {"id": "16:78/q04/p4", "position": "The initial hamza is omitted and the doubled mīm takes kasra.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAṭiyya and Abū Ḥayyān attribute this to al-Aʿmash; al-Ālūsī also reports it. Abū Ḥātim objects to deletion and says the mīm's kasra depended on the deleted hamza."}, {"id": "16:78/q04/p5", "position": "The initial hamza is omitted and the doubled mīm retains fatḥa.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAṭiyya and Abū Ḥayyān attribute this to Ibn Abī Laylā. Abū Ḥātim calls deletion poor but prefers the retained fatḥa to a kasra whose conditioning hamza was dropped. Al-Ālūsī repeats the judgment."}]}
{"id": "16:78/q05", "question": "What are the mothers' bellies here?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "16:78/q05/p1", "position": "They are the wombs from which children emerge.", "reasons": "Al-Suddī explicitly glosses the bellies as wombs."}]}
{"id": "16:78/q06", "question": "What does knowing nothing at birth encompass?", "turns_on": "Whether 'anything' is unrestricted, narrowed to a particular unknown, or restricted to acquired knowledge.", "positions": [{"id": "16:78/q06/p1", "position": "Newborn humans begin ignorant of things generally.", "reasons": "Muqātil, Ṭabarī, Wāḥidī, Ibn ʿAṭiyya, Rāzī, Bayḍāwī, Biqāʿī, Bursevī, and Study Quran state the broad ignorance. Abū Ḥayyān and al-Ālūsī prefer unrestricted wording, especially under negation. Bursevī includes worldly and afterlife matters and contrasts animal innate skills; Saʿdī's ant couplet makes the contrast. Study Quran pairs 16:70 and 30:54 on the rise and loss of knowledge. Al-Burhān uses it for ignorance preceding understanding."}, {"id": "16:78/q06/p2", "position": "It specifically means ignorance of the primordial covenant.", "reasons": "Al-Wāsiṭī invokes the 'Am I not your Lord?' covenant (7:172); Qurṭubī and al-Ālūsī locate it in the fathers' loins. Bursevī says people forget what souls or their atoms knew in the spirit world and covenant."}, {"id": "16:78/q06/p3", "position": "It means ignorance of one's decreed happiness or misery.", "reasons": "Sulamī's unnamed authority and Qushayrī mention one's unknown lot; Qurṭubī, Abū Ḥayyān, and al-Ālūsī transmit the limited interpretation. Qushayrī adds that God may turn an enemy or errant person into a saint, so no one knows their end."}, {"id": "16:78/q06/p4", "position": "It means ignorance of one's interests, benefits, or harms.", "reasons": "Qushayrī includes one's welfare; Ṭabrisī says benefits and harms; Qurṭubī, Abū Ḥayyān, and al-Ālūsī report the interests interpretation."}, {"id": "16:78/q06/p5", "position": "It means ignorance of the Benefactor's rights.", "reasons": "Al-Nasafī takes the clause circumstantially and ties the unknown rights to later gratitude, worship, and action."}, {"id": "16:78/q06/p6", "position": "It denies acquired sensory, imaginative, and intellectual knowledge, while leaving immediate self-awareness outside its scope.", "reasons": "Ṭabāṭabāʾī cites 16:70 on acquired knowledge and rejects the reading that would deny immediate self-knowledge."}]}
{"id": "16:78/q07", "question": "Does a person initially lack awareness of the self?", "turns_on": "Whether 'nothing' includes presential self-awareness and when the soul's blankness is placed.", "positions": [{"id": "16:78/q07/p1", "position": "Initial absence of knowledge includes even self-knowledge.", "reasons": "Some interlocutors of Ṭabāṭabāʾī draw this implication; al-Ālūsī rejects the alleged proof of invariable self-awareness as dependent on disputed claims that the soul is immaterial and all immaterial things know. Self-identity need not amount to knowing the soul's essence; awareness may require a condition. Al-Ṭūsī points to fainting and illness."}, {"id": "16:78/q07/p2", "position": "The soul has immediate awareness of itself even before acquired learning.", "reasons": "Philosophers reported by al-Ālūsī call this presential knowledge; the Shaykh argues one never loses it even asleep or intoxicated and uses it for an immaterial soul. Bahmanyār says the soul's existence is intellectual and its perception constitutes its existence, echoed in al-Shifāʾ. Ṭabāṭabāʾī excludes this from the verse's denial."}, {"id": "16:78/q07/p3", "position": "The blank state belongs to the soul before attachment to the body.", "reasons": "An unnamed scholar offers this to reconcile blankness with a baby's instinctive breast-seeking. Al-Ālūsī calls it strange because the proposed blank state would lie after bodily attachment yet before the behavior."}]}
{"id": "16:78/q08", "question": "How can knowledge arise after initial ignorance?", "turns_on": "Whether sensory experience itself yields cognitive basics, an Active Intellect supplies universals, or infant guidance comes by inspiration.", "positions": [{"id": "16:78/q08/p1", "position": "God teaches through senses and reasoning: sensed particulars yield conceptions and necessary judgments, then acquired knowledge.", "reasons": "Ṭabarī says reason distinguishes good and evil and memory preserves learning. Wāḥidī and Ibn ʿAṭiyya call senses a route or ladder. Rāzī divides knowledge into self-evident and acquired, raises the regress if axioms must be learned, and answers that sensory impressions produce conceptions which occasion axioms without prior learning; theoretical conclusions need proof. Bayḍāwī, Bursevī, and al-Ālūsī describe repeated perception, comparison, and reasoning. Elmalılı reads the verse as favoring empiricism and practice."}, {"id": "16:78/q08/p2", "position": "Particular sense impressions prepare the Active Intellect to impart universals.", "reasons": "Al-Ālūsī reports philosophers' four stages of intellect: potential, habitual, actual, and acquired; they hold that the soul itself does not perceive material particulars. He notes the long dispute."}, {"id": "16:78/q08/p3", "position": "Infants can be divinely inspired to suckle without instruction.", "reasons": "Qushayrī points to taking the mother's breast without prior warning, command, or rebuke; Bursevī contrasts humans' lack of the innate skills by which animals seek mother and food."}]}
{"id": "16:78/q09", "question": "What is reported about a newborn's earliest sensations?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "16:78/q09/p1", "position": "For seven days a newborn is ḥadhiran and perceives neither comfort nor pain.", "reasons": "Wahb's report is transmitted by Abū Ḥayyān and al-Ālūsī."}]}
{"id": "16:78/q10", "question": "How is لَا تَعْلَمُونَ شَيْـًۭٔا attached grammatically?", "turns_on": "Whether the note concerns the ḥāl within the birth clause or where that clause ends.", "positions": [{"id": "16:78/q10/p1", "position": "It is a circumstantial clause describing the people as they are brought out.", "reasons": "Ṭabrisī, Abū Ḥayyān, Samīn, and al-Ālūsī explicitly parse it as ḥāl; al-Nasafī also calls the newborn's lack of knowledge circumstantial."}, {"id": "16:78/q10/p2", "position": "The birth and ignorance clause ends at شيئا before a new clause on the faculties.", "reasons": "Ṭabarī, Thaʿlabī, Baghawī, and Qurṭubī mark this sentence boundary; Ṭabarī and Baghawī distinguish faculties created before birth from knowledge after it."}]}
{"id": "16:78/q11", "question": "How is شَيْـًۭٔا parsed?", "turns_on": "Whether شيء functions as the thing known or as a cognate accusative for knowledge itself.", "positions": [{"id": "16:78/q11/p1", "position": "It is the object of تعلمون, meaning 'recognize' or 'know'.", "reasons": "Ṭabrisī and Samīn allow the ordinary object. Al-ʿIzz objects that an ordinary 'know' with a cognate object would require two omitted objects and prior knowledge of the first. Al-Ālūsī replies that شيء can be the first object while only the second is omitted. Al-Burhān says cognitive علم takes meanings as objects."}, {"id": "16:78/q11/p2", "position": "It is an accusative cognate object, meaning 'any knowledge'.", "reasons": "Ṭabrisī and Samīn supply an implied لا تعلمون علما. {"id": "16:78/q12", "question": "How does وَجَعَلَ relate to أَخْرَجَكُم?", "turns_on": "Whether the conjunction joins predicates within one report or starts a new report.", "positions": [{"id": "16:78/q12/p1", "position": "It may coordinate with أخرجكم within the same report about God.", "reasons": "Wāḥidī says waw does not impose time order. Abū Ḥayyān, Samīn, and al-Ālūsī explicitly allow coordination within the predicate; Bursevī reports that the faculties' effects appear after birth though they existed potentially earlier."}, {"id": "16:78/q12/p2", "position": "It may begin an independent clause coordinated with the opening statement.", "reasons": "Ṭabarī, Thaʿlabī, Baghawī, and Qurṭubī end the prior statement at شيئا; Abū Ḥayyān, Samīn, and al-Ālūsī also allow an independent new report."}]}
{"id": "16:78/q13", "question": "Does the order of bringing out and giving faculties imply when the faculties were created?", "turns_on": "Whether the wording refers to creation of the faculties or to their later exercise.", "positions": [{"id": "16:78/q13/p1", "position": "No: the faculties were made before birth, while knowledge or their effective use comes after birth.", "reasons": "Ṭabarī, Thaʿlabī, Baghawī, and Qurṭubī distinguish prenatal faculties from postnatal knowledge or grant. Wāḥidī and Rāzī say waw has no temporal force; Abū ʿUbayda says Arabic may reverse listed events, and Ibn al-Jawzī adduces a line naming lesser assessed dues before greater. Bursevī's al-Irshād treats the powers as potential until their later effects; al-Ālūsī similarly emphasizes activation."}, {"id": "16:78/q13/p2", "position": "Hearing and sight may name the acts of listening and seeing, which occur after birth.", "reasons": "Rāzī offers this as another solution to the apparent chronological objection."}]}
{"id": "16:78/q14", "question": "How many objects does جَعَلَ take here?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "16:78/q14/p1", "position": "It takes one object if it means 'create', but two if it means 'render', with لكم the second.", "reasons": "Al-Ālūsī gives the two grammatical construals."}]}
{"id": "16:78/q15", "question": "What are the faculties given for?", "turns_on": "Whether the faculties are explained as routes to knowledge generally, as ways to receive divine guidance, or as capable of failing that purpose.", "positions": [{"id": "16:78/q15/p1", "position": "They are instruments of perception and acquisition of knowledge.", "reasons": "Ṭabarī details sound, conversation, sight, recognition, retention, and reflection. Ṭabrisī calls the senses sound routes to percepts and hearts the seat of understanding. Abū Ḥayyān says organ names stand for faculties, with hearing and sight for sensibles and reason for intelligibles. Rāzī, Bayḍāwī, Bursevī, al-Ālūsī, Ṭabāṭabāʾī, and Kur'an Yolu explain the move from particulars to thought; Ṭabāṭabāʾī includes touch, taste, and smell."}, {"id": "16:78/q15/p2", "position": "They receive revelation and moral admonition, perceive God's signs and blessings, and know His greatness.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAbbās, Qushayrī, Sulamī's Abū ʿUthmān, Qurṭubī, and the commentators reported by Rāzī pair hearing with divine address or commands, sight with divine acts, and hearts with the Maker. Al-Ālūsī also reports hearing Qurʾān and Sunna as transmitted proofs and seeing created wonders; he insists the outward senses retain their ordinary meanings. Study Quran relates the grouping to guidance and cites 22:46 and, for gifts, 10:31, 23:78, 32:9."}, {"id": "16:78/q15/p3", "position": "They can become impaired or impervious to guidance.", "reasons": "Study Quran cites 2:7, 6:25, 6:110, 7:179, and 18:57."}]}
{"id": "16:78/q16", "question": "Why is ٱلسَّمْع singular while ٱلْأَبْصَٰر and ٱلْأَفْـِٔدَةَ are plural?", "turns_on": "Whether the singular follows the word's grammatical class, its collective force, or differences in the faculties' objects.", "positions": [{"id": "16:78/q16/p1", "position": "سمع is a verbal noun or generic collective and thus remains singular.", "reasons": "Jishumī and Bursevī call it a verbal noun; Jishumī also reports the generic noun view. Ibn al-Jawzī says the singular form refers collectively and points to 2:7; al-Ālūsī gives the verbal-noun explanation."}, {"id": "16:78/q16/p2", "position": "Hearing has one kind of object, while sight has many.", "reasons": "Al-Ālūsī reports this account of singular versus plural."}, {"id": "16:78/q16/p3", "position": "Sight and hearts vary more greatly than hearing.", "reasons": "Biqāʿī suggests this while acknowledging that only God knows the full extent of the variation."}]}
{"id": "16:78/q17", "question": "Why is hearing mentioned before sight?", "turns_on": "Whether primacy is assigned to revelation, development, or the number of objects perceived.", "positions": [{"id": "16:78/q17/p1", "position": "Hearing receives revelation and divine speech.", "reasons": "Bursevī adds that some prophets lost sight but not hearing; al-Ālūsī reports receiving revelation as an explanation."}, {"id": "16:78/q17/p2", "position": "Hearing develops before sight in a newborn.", "reasons": "Bursevī says newborn eyes open later; al-Ālūsī reports the developmental explanation."}, {"id": "16:78/q17/p3", "position": "Audible objects are fewer.", "reasons": "Al-Ālūsī reports this as another ordering rationale."}]}
{"id": "16:78/q18", "question": "Why do hearing and sight precede the heart?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "16:78/q18/p1", "position": "Outward perception supplies or precedes inward understanding.", "reasons": "Al-Ālūsī says the outward senses contribute to the heart's cognition; another comparison makes senses servants preceding the master, with fewer objects than the heart's almost innumerable objects, though sight and intellect both have limits. {"id": "16:78/q19", "question": "What does the choice of hearing and sight imply about other senses?", "turns_on": "Whether the named senses represent sensory knowledge broadly or bear on a disputed theory of internal senses.", "positions": [{"id": "16:78/q19/p1", "position": "It emphasizes these two while the senses also include touch, taste, and smell.", "reasons": "Ṭabāṭabāʾī lists those other senses as starting points for conceptions; Rāzī says other senses likewise supply particulars."}, {"id": "16:78/q19/p2", "position": "Some take the pair as evidence against philosophers' five internal senses.", "reasons": "Al-Ālūsī reports the inference and says it needs fuller discussion."}]}
